clinicalPearls: A form of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism combined with impaired or absent sense of smell (anosmia or hyposmia)
Results from defective embryonic migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons alongside the olfactory nerves
Genetically heterogeneous, with X-linked ANOS1 and autosomal genes such as FGFR1 among the recognised causes
Typically presents as absent or incomplete puberty with low sex steroids and inappropriately low or normal gonadotropins
Associated features vary by gene and can include midline defects such as cleft lip or palate, dental agenesis, and unilateral renal agenesis
Synkinesia (mirror movements) is a recognised feature of some X-linked cases
Fertility can often be achieved with gonadotropin therapy or pulsatile GnRH, distinguishing it from primary gonadal failure
reference.pathophysiology: During development, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate along the olfactory nerve fibres to reach the hypothalamus. In Kallmann syndrome, mutations affecting the genes that guide this migration disrupt both the olfactory pathway and the arrival of GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus. The resulting deficiency of hypothalamic GnRH leads to reduced pituitary secretion of luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormones and consequent hypogonadism, while the shared developmental defect explains the coexisting impairment of smell.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from illness, stress or excessive exercise
Hyperprolactinaemia or other pituitary lesions suppressing gonadotropins
additionalInvestigations: Basal luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and sex steroid measurement
Formal or structured assessment of the sense of smell
Pituitary and hypothalamic MRI, which may show olfactory bulb hypoplasia or aplasia
Molecular genetic testing of ANOS1, FGFR1 and other associated genes
Renal imaging and screening for associated midline or skeletal anomalies
redFlags: Features suggesting an expanding pituitary or hypothalamic mass rather than a congenital defect
Associated anomalies such as renal agenesis or midline defects requiring dedicated evaluation
Absence of any pubertal progression by the expected age warranting prompt endocrine assessment
Signs of broader pituitary hormone deficiency indicating combined hypopituitarism
reference.prognosis: With appropriate hormone replacement, secondary sexual characteristics and bone health can be maintained, and fertility is frequently achievable with gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy; a minority experience reversal of the hypogonadism.
pitfalls: Attributing delayed puberty to constitutional delay and missing a genuine congenital deficiency
Failing to test the sense of smell, which is a key discriminating clinical feature
Overlooking associated anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis
Assuming infertility is irreversible rather than treatable with gonadotropin therapy
management: Replace sex steroids, with testosterone in males and oestrogen-progestogen in females, to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and bone health
Induce fertility when desired with gonadotropin therapy or pulsatile GnRH
Monitor and optimise bone mineral density given the hypogonadism
Screen for associated anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis, cleft lip or palate and dental agenesis
Offer genetic counselling with testing of ANOS1, FGFR1 and other associated genes
Coordinate multidisciplinary endocrinology, fertility and clinical genetics care with psychological support
